text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Random Experiments, Outcomes, and Sample Spaces",
    "scope": "Introduces the foundational objects of probability theory: random experiments, individual outcomes, and the sample space S. Classifies sample spaces by cardinality into finite, countably infinite, and uncountably infinite domains using physical and engineering examples. Demonstrates how multiple sample spaces of differing granularity can model the same physical experiment depending on the observation goal.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of random experiment, elementary outcome omega, and universal sample space S",
      "Classification of sample spaces: finite (coin toss {H, T}, die {1, ..., 6}), countably infinite (packet arrivals {0, 1, 2, ...}), and uncountably infinite (component lifetime [0, infty), particle coordinates R^3)",
      "Granularity principle: multiple valid sample spaces exist for an experiment (e.g., exact die face {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} vs. parity {even, odd})"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Events, Set Operations, and Algebraic Identities",
    "scope": "Defines an event as a subset of the sample space, distinguishing elementary, compound, certain, and impossible (null) events. Establishes set-theoretic operations for event manipulation: complement, union, intersection, set difference, and mutual exclusivity. Formulates fundamental boolean set identities and presents an element-wise logical proof of De Morgan's laws.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of an event A as a subset of S, elementary vs compound events, S as certain event, and empty set emptyset as impossible event",
      "Event operations: union A cup B (or), intersection A cap B (and), complement A^c (not), difference A setminus B (A and not B)",
      "Mutual exclusivity: A and B are disjoint if A cap B = emptyset",
      "Fundamental identities: A cap emptyset = emptyset, A cup emptyset = A, A cap A^c = emptyset, A cup A^c = S, (A^c)^c = A",
      "De Morgan's laws: (A cap B)^c = A^c cup B^c and (A cup B)^c = A^c cap B^c with element-wise logical proofs"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "Empirical and Classical Models of Probability",
    "scope": "Develops the transition from experimental frequency observations to the classical discrete probability model. Explains the empirical relative frequency definition, its convergence to true probability as trials n approach infinity, and the statistical stabilization of heads in repeated coin tosses. Defines the classical Laplace model for finite sample spaces with equally likely outcomes and specifies its structural limitations.",
    "key_points": [
      "Empirical relative frequency: P(A) approx m / n where m is occurrences across n independent trials",
      "Frequency stabilization principle: empirical convergence as n -> infty (stabilization from error 10^-1 at n=10^2 to 10^-3 at n=10^6)",
      "Classical definition: P(A) = |A| / |S| = m / n for finite sample spaces with equally likely outcomes",
      "Limitations: empirical probability requires repeatable trials; classical model strictly requires symmetry and finite sample spaces"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "Discrete Probability Spaces with Non-Uniform Weights",
    "scope": "Extends discrete probability beyond the equally likely paradigm to weighted discrete outcome spaces. Formulates the total probability weight condition where the sum of elementary probabilities must equal unity. Demonstrates probability computation by aggregating elementary weights on biased spaces, such as loaded dice.",
    "key_points": [
      "Assignment of individual outcome weights w_i = P({omega_i}) satisfying w_i >= 0 and sum_i w_i = 1",
      "Probability of an event A as the sum of weights: P(A) = sum_{omega in A} P({omega})",
      "Biased system modeling: setting up weight equations (e.g., even faces twice as likely as odd faces yielding 9w = 1, w = 1/9)",
      "Calculating compound event probabilities via weighted summation"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "Geometric Probability on Continuous Domains",
    "scope": "Generalizes classical probability to uncountable continuous sample spaces represented as measurable subsets of Euclidean space R^n. Defines geometric probability as the ratio of Lebesgue measures: length, area, or volume under uniform distribution. Solves classic geometric problems including the Alice-Bob meeting problem with waiting time thresholds and the broken stick problem using linear bounding inequalities.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: P(A) = measure(A) / measure(S) for length (R^1), area (R^2), or volume (R^3)",
      "Meeting problem: uniform independent arrivals x, y in [0, 60] on S = [0, 60]^2; condition |x - y| <= t",
      "Area-complement method: P(Meeting) = 1 - ((60 - t)/60)^2; evaluation at t = 15 yields P = 7/16 = 0.4375, and solving for P >= 1/2 gives t >= 60 - 30*sqrt(2) approx 17.57 minutes",
      "Broken stick problem: breaking [0, 1] at x, y; triangle inequality requires all pieces < 1/2, yielding successful area 1/8 + 1/8 = 1/4"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Sigma-Algebras and Measurable Spaces",
    "scope": "Provides the mathematical motivation for sigma-algebras when infinite sample spaces contain non-measurable subsets. Formulates the axiomatic definition of a sigma-algebra on a sample space S and defines the measurable space pair (S, F). Catalogs fundamental sigma-algebras: trivial, power set, generated by finite partitions (2^n elements), Borel sigma-algebra on R, and countable-cocountable algebras.",
    "key_points": [
      "Need for sigma-algebras: preventing non-measurable sets / paradoxes when assigning probabilities on infinite sets",
      "Definition of sigma-algebra F: S in F; closed under complements (A in F implies A^c in F); closed under countable unions (A_i in F implies union_{i=1}^infty A_i in F)",
      "Measurable space: the pair (S, F)",
      "Catalog of sigma-algebras: trivial F_0 = {emptyset, S}, power set P(S) = 2^S, generated algebra sigma(A) = {emptyset, A, A^c, S}",
      "Algebra generated by a partition: a partition of n atoms generates an algebra of size 2^n",
      "Continuous and infinite structures: Borel sigma-algebra B(R) generated by open intervals (a, b), countable-cocountable sigma-algebra"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Algebraic Properties and Operations on Sigma-Algebras",
    "scope": "Investigates closure properties under set-theoretic operations applied to multiple sigma-algebras. Proves that the arbitrary intersection of sigma-algebras is always a valid sigma-algebra. Demonstrates via concrete finite counterexamples why the union of two sigma-algebras is generally not a sigma-algebra due to the failure of closure under unions.",
    "key_points": [
      "Theorem: If F_1 and F_2 are sigma-algebras on S, their intersection F_1 cap F_2 is a sigma-algebra",
      "Step-by-step verification of intersection: contains S, closed under complements, closed under countable unions",
      "Theorem: The union F_1 cup F_2 of two sigma-algebras is generally not a sigma-algebra",
      "Counterexample: On X = {1, 2, 3}, F_1 = {emptyset, {1}, {2, 3}, X} and F_2 = {emptyset, {2}, {1, 3}, X} are sigma-algebras, but {1} cup {2} = {1, 2} notin F_1 cup F_2"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "Kolmogorov Axioms and Probability Spaces",
    "scope": "Presents Kolmogorov's axiomatic foundation of modern probability theory. Defines a probability measure as a mapping from a sigma-algebra to the real numbers satisfying non-negativity, normalization, and countable additivity, defining the probability space triple (S, F, P). Evaluates whether candidate set functions on finite and countable spaces satisfy these axioms and determines normalization constants for convergent series.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of probability space as the triple (S, F, P)",
      "Kolmogorov Axiom 1 (Non-negativity): P(A) >= 0 for all A in F",
      "Kolmogorov Axiom 2 (Normalization): P(S) = 1",
      "Kolmogorov Axiom 3 (Countable Additivity): P(bigcup_{i=1}^infty A_i) = sum_{i=1}^infty P(A_i) for pairwise disjoint A_i",
      "Axiom verification on finite sets: identifying violations of normalization, non-negativity, and additivity",
      "Axiom verification on countable sets: geometric weight distribution P({k}) = c / 3^k normalized by c = 2; failure of purely finite/infinite indicator measures to satisfy additivity"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "title": "Fundamental Consequences of the Kolmogorov Axioms",
    "scope": "Derives the core mathematical properties of probability measures rigorously from Kolmogorov's three axioms. Proves that the impossible event has zero measure, establishes the complement rule, and demonstrates monotonicity with the difference rule. Formulates finite additivity and Boole's inequality (union bound) for general collections of events.",
    "key_points": [
      "Probability of empty set: P(emptyset) = 0 via P(S cup emptyset) = P(S) + P(emptyset) = 1",
      "Complement rule: P(A^c) = 1 - P(A) via S = A cup A^c with A cap A^c = emptyset",
      "Difference rule: P(B setminus A) = P(B) - P(A cap B); if A subseteq B, P(B setminus A) = P(B) - P(A)",
      "Monotonicity: A subseteq B implies P(A) <= P(B), proven by B = A sqcup (B setminus A) and P(B setminus A) >= 0",
      "Boole's inequality (Union Bound): P(bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i) <= sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i) for arbitrary events"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 10,
    "title": "Addition Rules and the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion",
    "scope": "Extends additivity to non-disjoint events through the addition rule and the general principle of inclusion-exclusion. Proves the two-event addition formula and its corollary for mutually exclusive sets. Develops the three-event inclusion-exclusion formula and techniques for evaluating composite event configurations, including exactly one, at least two, and symmetric difference.",
    "key_points": [
      "Two-event addition rule: P(A cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A cap B) with proof correcting for double-counted intersection",
      "Mutual exclusivity corollary: P(A cup B) = P(A) + P(B) when A cap B = emptyset",
      "Three-event inclusion-exclusion formula: P(A cup B cup C) = sum P(A) - sum P(A cap B) + P(A cap B cap C)",
      "Symmetric difference: P(A Delta B) = P((A setminus B) cup (B setminus A)) = P(A cup B) - P(A cap B)",
      "Multi-event combinatorial structures: computing 'at least two' as sum_{i<j} P(A_i cap A_j) - 2*P(A cap B cap C), and 'exactly one' as P(A cup B cup C) - P(at least two)"
    ]
  }
]
